Differential diagnoses included chicken pox, pityriasis lichenoides varioliformis acuta, dermatitis herpetiformis, Sweet syndrome, bacterial folliculitis, and lymphomatoid papulosis. A skin biopsy of the lesion was performed. The epidermis showed crustation, exocytosis of neutrophils, and multiple intraepidermal abscesses. The dermis showed heavy cellular infiltrates composed mainly of neutrophils (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: e no similar attacks before and no history of contact with a similar condition. The patient had a positive history of using iodine and bromide food supplements for four months prior to the appearance of skin rashes. An allergy history, surgical history, medical history, family history, and review of systems were all unremarkable. The patient did not experience any symptoms of iodism such as mouth burning or increased salivation, metallic taste, tooth and gum soreness, and headache. Skin examination revealed multiple crusted papules and nodules scattered on his face, neck, and trunk (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: The image is a Hematoxylin-Eosin stained section of skin from an infant with confirmed Bromoderma (Halogenoderma). The caption details the pathological findings: pseudoepitheliomatous acanthosis, parakeratosis, and both eosinophilic and neutrophilic dermal infiltrates, which directly correlate with the known histological manifestations of the disease.
panels.attribution_text: Hoefel et al. Bromoderma in an infant.. Anais brasileiros de dermatologia 2016. doi:10.1590/abd1806-4841.20165013. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: Skin presenting pseudoepitheliomatous acanthosis, keratosis and parakeratosis. Bleeding and eosinophilic and neutrophilic infiltrate in the papillary dermis. Hematoxylin-eosin 45X
in_text_mentions: ere within normal limits. The infant was fed with infant formula. The mother reported that the infant had colic since the first month of life and was receiving daily colic medication and, occasionally, paracetamol. The active ingredient in the colic syrup - a compounded medication - was calcium bromide. Based on clinical findings and on the intake of bromide-containing syrup history, we diagnosed bromoderma. Our diagnosis was later confirmed by pathological examination (Figure 5). Skin lesions regressed slowly in the next 15 days after the drug withdrawal and disappeared in 30 days (Figure 6).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows pinpoint pustules on the chest of a patient diagnosed with Iododerma (a form of Halogenoderma) following contrast administration. B: Panel B shows deep red mottling of the thighs, which is a diffuse erythematous manifestation of the patient's Halogenoderma.
panels.attribution_text: Truong et al. Delayed Hypersensitivity to Iodinated Contrast: A Rare Case of Iododerma and Successful Strategy for Readministration.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112105. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Hundreds of pinpoint pustules on the chest (A) and deep red mottling of the thighs (B)
in_text_mentions: Five hours after the angiogram, she developed pruritic, erythematous papules on her back and was treated with intravenous diphenhydramine. The rash progressed into diffuse erythema involving the face, trunk, arms, and thighs, with hundreds of pinpoint erythematous pustules distributed across the face and chest (Figure 2). Additional erythematous papules were noted on the extremities. There was also non-pitting edema of the bilateral hands, forearms, feet, and shins.
